title: Fitts’ Law, GOMS, and Responsible Early Estimates

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Fitts’ Law, GOMS, and Responsible Early Estimates.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Predictive interaction models estimate aspects of skilled physical and procedural performance. They are useful because teams can compare alternatives early and identify avoidable work. They are limited because human activity also includes perception, comprehension, learning, uncertainty, emotion, collaboration, error, interruption, disability, and meaning.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Models reduce a bounded kind of uncertainty
turns.text: What changes when we look at models reduce a bounded kind of uncertainty?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Fitts’ Law models pointing time as a function of distance to a target and its effective width in the direction of movement. A common form is:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: MT = a + b × log₂(D / W + 1)

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: MT is movement time, D is distance, W is target width, and a and b are empirically fitted for a device and context. The logarithmic term is an index of difficulty. Larger targets and shorter travel generally support faster selection.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Screen edges can act as effectively deep targets for a pointer because the cursor cannot overshoot—but that advantage does not automatically transfer to touch, eye gaze, switch control, or spatially separated devices.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Fitts’ Law does not tell whether the target is noticed, understood, safe, or reachable by keyboard. Visual size may differ from effective interactive size. Nearby destructive actions may increase errors even if movement is fast.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: GOMS represents routine work through Goals, Operators, Methods, and Selection rules. A goal such as “resolve missing referral data” can have several methods; selection rules describe when an experienced user chooses each.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The Keystroke-Level Model (KLM) estimates a learned, error-free method using operators such as keystrokes, pointing, homing between devices, mental preparation, and system response.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: These models are strongest for stable, frequent, skilled tasks with known methods. They are weak for discovery, learning, interpretation, variable AI output, collaboration, error recovery, and situations where people invent strategies as they go.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at conduct a responsible comparison?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: 1. Define the user, expertise, device, environment, task, starting state, and successful end state. 2. Write each plausible method as an observable sequence. Include system waits and device switching. 3. Apply only the model whose assumptions fit. Use locally measured constants where precision matters. 4.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Report a range and relative difference rather than false universal precision. 5. Mark model boundaries—decision, search, interruption, error, collaboration, or interpretation. 6. Predict side effects such as accidental activation, reduced discoverability, accessibility barriers, or increased training. 7.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Validate consequential changes with representative people and realistic work.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Analytical models can eliminate obviously inefficient options or direct attention. They cannot establish desirability, safety, or outcome.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: creative software?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A keyboard shortcut may outperform a menu in a KLM estimate for expert repetition. Novices may not discover it, users with motor impairments may find the chord inaccessible, and accidental activation may be costly. A responsible design can provide menu visibility, remapping, undo, and progressive shortcut discovery.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The model supports an expert accelerator; it does not justify removing the learnable path.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Click-count simplification: all actions are treated as equal. False constants: textbook timings are presented as local measurements. Model beyond boundary: search, judgement, error, or collaboration is squeezed into precise estimates. Average operator: capability, device, expertise, and context variation disappears.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Speed as outcome: faster interaction is assumed to be better despite errors or reduced deliberation. Optimisation trap: one local task improves while the end-to-end service worsens.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Use models to compare designs, not certify them
turns.text: What changes when we look at use models to compare designs, not certify them?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The estimates exclude many decisive factors: learning, visual search, comprehension, emotion, collaboration, fatigue, accessibility, error recovery, system latency, and service consequence. A faster shortcut can be unsafe; a larger target can encourage premature action; a predicted time saving may disappear under real queue interruptions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Models narrow design candidates and identify questions for evaluation.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team verifies with observation and performance data across relevant input methods and people. Prediction error is recorded and the model updated or discarded. Senior practice reports both estimated benefit and the conditions under which it holds rather than presenting a precise number as scientific certainty.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: warehouse picking?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Movement modelling can compare scanner controls and item confirmation, but cannot capture aisle congestion, packaging variation, fatigue, or exception judgment. Combining the estimate with field observation prevents a locally faster interface from slowing the whole operation.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior practitioners decide where efficiency is ethical. Faster is valuable for high-volume clerical work, but deliberation may protect informed consent, safety, or financial judgement. Document model version, assumptions, constants, task method, excluded behaviour, and sensitivity to changes.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Where an estimate influences staffing or investment, validate it under real conditions and include variability rather than a single impressive number.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a warehouse scanning tool. A smaller target farther from the user's thumb may increase selection effort; a long, branching flow adds steps to a repeated task. Fitts' Law and GOMS can help compare early options under stated assumptions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Validate those estimates with real devices, gloves, movement, error recovery, and the actual work environment before treating them as performance facts.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Compare two ways to perform the same action. Identify distance, target size, device changes, mental preparation, and system wait. Then list three important aspects of the experience the estimate cannot represent.
